claims.assert: D['quarters'][41]['year'] == 2022 and D['quarters'][41]['q'] == 2 and round(sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][38:42]) / 4 * 100, 1) == 16.7 and close(max(sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) / 4 for i in range(3, len(D['quarters']))), sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][38:42]) / 4, 1e-12)
claims.actual: max((sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) / 4, D['quarters'][i]['year'], D['quarters'][i]['q']) for i in range(3, len(D['quarters'])))
claims.falsified_if: The maximum lands in another quarter or off 16.65-16.75. The peak is labeled on the chart by value and by year, so a shift breaks both.

claims.text: Hiring bottomed at 1,373 in 2020Q2 and peaked at 4,106 in 2022Q1.
claims.source: Census QWI HirA, PIC-12 summed
claims.assert: min(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) == 1373 and max(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) == 4106 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 1373)['year'] == 2020 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 1373)['q'] == 2 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 4106)['year'] == 2022 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 4106)['q'] == 1 and one(q for q in D['quarters'] if q['hires'] == 1373)['seps'] == 1872
claims.actual: (min(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']), max(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']))
claims.falsified_if: Either extreme moves to another quarter, or 2020Q2's separations move off 1,872. Both quarters are named in the flow chart's annotation, and the annotation is the section's claim about the pandemic years.

claims.text: Between 2012 and the last four published quarters the leaving (separation) rate rose about 1.9 points and the hiring (hire) rate about 0.2.
claims.source: derived: hires/jobs and separations/jobs, four-quarter means at each end
claims.assert: round((sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, 1) == 1.9 and round((sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, 1) == 0.2 and round((sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4 - sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, 1) == 0.9
claims.actual: ((sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100, (sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 - sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][:4]) / 4) * 100)
claims.falsified_if: Either component moves by a tenth of a point, or the two stop summing to twice the headline churn gap. This is the page's third act: if the hire-side rise turns out to be the larger one, the section title, the lede and the chart all assert the opposite of the data. IDENTIFICATION: this is a decomposition of an identity, not an explanation — nothing here says why people are leaving.

claims.text: Averaged over a year, separations have run above hires in each of the eleven quarters since 2023Q1.
claims.source: derived: separation rate minus hire rate, trailing four quarters
claims.assert: D['quarters'][44]['year'] == 2023 and D['quarters'][44]['q'] == 1 and all(sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) > sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) for i in range(44, len(D['quarters']))) and sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][40:44]) < sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][40:44]) and len(D['quarters']) - 44 == 11
claims.actual: [(D['quarters'][i]['year'], D['quarters'][i]['q'], round((sum(q['seps']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1]) - sum(q['hires']/q['emp'] for q in D['quarters'][i-3:i+1])) / 4 * 100, 2)) for i in range(42, len(D['quarters']))]
claims.falsified_if: Any quarter from 2023Q1 on flips sign, or 2022Q4 stops being the last quarter on the hiring-ahead side. The run length is printed in the section's fig-title and in the closer, so a broken run breaks both. A single flipped quarter also means the phrase 'in every quarter since' has to go.

claims.text: County rates run from 6.2% in Mahoning to 13.5% in Trumbull, and nine of the twelve recorded more separations than hires.
claims.source: Census QWI by county, last four published quarters
claims.assert: len(D['counties']) == 12 and round(max(c['churn_rate'] for c in D['counties']) * 100, 1) == 13.5 and one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['churn_rate'] == max(x['churn_rate'] for x in D['counties']))['county'] == 'Trumbull' and round(min(c['churn_rate'] for c in D['counties']) * 100, 1) == 6.2 and one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['churn_rate'] == min(x['churn_rate'] for x in D['counties']))['county'] == 'Mahoning' and sum(1 for c in D['counties'] if c['seps'] > c['hires']) == 9
claims.actual: sorted((round(c['churn_rate'] * 100, 1), c['county']) for c in D['counties'])
claims.falsified_if: The extremes change county or move a tenth of a point, or the outflow count leaves 9. SMALL NUMBERS: Trumbull's rate rests on 402 jobs, so it is the cell most likely to move on revision and the one the chart annotates as 'high rate, small base'. The default verdict sentence under the county selector prints all three numbers.

claims.text: Trumbull runs 434 starts and ends in a year on 402 jobs: at 13.5%, about 54 of its jobs start in a quarter and about 54 end. Summit runs 2,644 on 4,019 jobs, 6.1 times Trumbull's.
claims.source: Census QWI by county, last four published quarters
claims.assert: one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Trumbull')['hires'] + one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Trumbull')['seps'] == 434 and one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Summit')['hires'] + one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Summit')['seps'] == 2644 and one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Trumbull')['emp'] == 402 and one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Summit')['emp'] == 4019 and max(c['emp'] for c in D['counties']) == 4019 and round(2644 / 434, 1) == 6.1 and round(one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Trumbull')['churn_rate'] * 402) == 54 and abs(one(c for c in D['counties'] if c['county'] == 'Trumbull')['churn_rate'] * 402 * 8 - 434) < 3
claims.actual: [(c['county'], c['emp'], round(c['churn_rate'] * c['emp']), c['hires'] + c['seps']) for c in D['counties']]
claims.falsified_if: Either county's event count or employment moves, or some other county overtakes Summit on employment (the assertion pins that too, because the chart annotates Summit as the largest base), or 13.5% of 402 stops rounding to 54 a quarter, or the per-quarter figure times eight stops landing within three events of 434. THE ARITHMETIC HAS TO CLOSE ON THE PAGE. The annotation used to read '13.5% of 402 jobs is 434 job events', which hides a multiplier of eight — four quarters, and both sides of the flow. A naive reader multiplied, got 54, assumed a typo, and distrusted the page for two passes. The percentage now lives on the y-axis and in one fig-sub sentence that spells out the 54 and the ×8 in words; the on-chart annotations print counts only, and the one derived figure left on the chart (6.1) divides 2,644 by 434, both of which are printed beside it. This pair is the whole rate-versus-base argument, drawn as two annotated dots.

claims.text: At a 150-person plant, the current 9.6% quarterly churn is about fourteen hires and fourteen departures a quarter, five of each in a month, and about 58 replacement hires a year; the 55-quarter average of 10.8% is sixteen and sixteen, and about 65 a year.
claims.source: derived: the recent four-quarter and the 55-quarter mean churn rates applied to a 150-person payroll
claims.assert: round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4) == 14 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 / 3) == 5 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 * 4) == 58 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters'])) == 16 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) / 3) == 5 and round(150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) * 4) == 65
claims.actual: (150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4, 150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters'][-4:]) / 4 * 4, 150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']), 150 * sum(q['churn_rate'] for q in D['quarters']) / len(D['quarters']) * 4)
claims.falsified_if: Any of the six numbers moves by one. ORDER MATTERS AND IS GUARDED HERE: the section used to open on 10.8%, the highest and least current of the three churn figures on the page, and conceded the current 9.6% in its last sentence. A reader holding three churn numbers at once was handed the stalest one first. The heading, the lede and the translator's default sentence now lead with the last four published quarters and offer the 55-quarter average as the comparison, so both pairs of numbers are asserted. Other headcounts typed into the translator are the same arithmetic and are unguarded by design. ILLUSTRATIVE: it applies a cluster average to a single site and is not a measurement of any plant.

claims.text: The region started 6.0 times its own opening workforce, and the 222,890 hire and separation events are about 1,327 for every one job of the 168-job margin between starts and ends.
claims.source: derived: total hires over opening employment; total events over net
claims.assert: round(sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) / D['quarters'][0]['emp'], 1) == 6.0 and sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) + sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']) == 222890 and round((sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) + sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters'])) / (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters']))) == 1327
claims.actual: (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) / D['quarters'][0]['emp'], (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) + sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters'])) / (sum(q['hires'] for q in D['quarters']) - sum(q['seps'] for q in D['quarters'])))
claims.falsified_if: The multiple leaves 5.95-6.05 or the ratio leaves 1,322-1,332. The ratio is unstable by construction: its denominator is a small difference of two large numbers, so a revision of a few hundred events moves it by hundreds. That fragility is the reason the closer says 'about'.
